title: רבה א) <small>(סתם הוא)</small> בר נחמני
author: Heilprin source tradition; Warsaw digital witness

paragraphs: Rabbah. (1) Without further qualification, he is bar Nahmani (so Halikhot Olam writes). His brother was Kaylil, Abaye's father (see there): Bava Batra folio 8; end of Ketubbot. He was of Eli's house, lived forty years, and was a priest (see what I wrote under Rava). In Helek 98b, Rabbah said, ‘Let him come, but may I not see him.’ Abaye asked, ‘Why does the master say this?’ etc. ‘The master has Torah and acts of kindness.’ Ri [ר״י; personal identification unresolved here] said that he did not engage in kindness sufficiently to be saved from the decree upon Eli's house, as Abaye did, engaging in Torah and kindness and living sixty years. But he had enough to be saved from the messianic birth-pangs. In Yuhasin [Amoraim by Their Times, third generation], Zacut reports the pious man’s chronology: Rav Huna died in year 50 of the fifth millennium, Rav Hisda in year 60; Rabbah succeeded him for twenty-two years, lived forty years, and died in year 82 of the fifth millennium. According to this reckoning he was born three years after R' Yohanan's death. Zacut objects: at the end of Ketubbot, 111, end of a, his brothers in the Land of Israel—R' Hanina and R' Hoshaya, see there—sent him word to come there too: ‘If you say you have no teacher, you do have a teacher: R' Yohanan.’ He must have been at least eighteen or twenty when his brothers sent to him—otherwise how could they say ‘If you have no teacher’? Moreover, all agree that Rabbah was Rav Huna's pupil (see there and above). According to this reckoning, with Rav Huna dying in 50 and Rabbah in 82, Rabbah was eight years old—that is, since his whole life was forty years, when he studied before Rav Huna, before Rav Huna's death, he was only eight. This is impossible. Another difficulty: he says Rabbah received from Rav Yehudah, which is true, as is evident at the beginning of Shemonah Sheratzim (see below). The difficulty is then greater, since Rav Yehudah died before Rav Huna: both academies returned to Rav Huna when Rav Yehudah died, as he himself writes. Rabbah was thus older when he received from Rav Huna. It therefore appears that the pious man's tradition here is incorrect. Rather, Rabbah and Rav Hisda headed academies concurrently: Rabbah at Pumbedita—Rashi, Megillah 7, beginning of b—after Rav Yehudah; Rav Hisda at Sura after Rav Huna. Rav Huna died in year 60, and Rabbah was then eighteen, fit for ordination, when his brothers sent him their letter. He presided twenty-two years immediately after Rav Huna died. Reason suggests that R' Yohanan and Rav Yehudah died then, or a year earlier, since Rav Yehudah was very old. Rabbah would therefore also have lived in Rav Yehudah's time, and began presiding immediately after Rav Yehudah's death, as Ha-Nizzakin says: ‘That shofar which was in Rav Yehudah's house, and afterward in Rabbah's house.’ Rashi explains: Rav Yehudah was head of the academy at Pumbedita; when he died and Rabbah began presiding, they placed it in his house. In Tosafot, Ha-Mafkid, it appears that Rabbah judged in Rav Hisda's time. If Rav Yehudah died before Rav Huna, Rabbah began presiding before Rav Hisda, contrary to Dorot Olam's statement that Rabbah presided after Rav Hisda. The Talmud also always mentions ‘Rabbah and Rav Hisda.’ End quotation. See Yuhasin, Rav Sherira Gaon's Epistle, and what I wrote in Part I, 4234.

Tosafot, Eruvin 22b: Rabbah went to the Land of Israel to study Torah with R' Yohanan, as found at the end of Ketubbot—his brothers sent him word to come, as above. But we have not found that Abaye went and studied before R' Yohanan. Tosafot, Yevamot 78a, likewise write this. Tosafot, Bava Batra 155a: ‘We read Rabbah,’ since R' Assi told him, ‘Rabbi, do you say this?’ Rava did not go to the Land of Israel, whereas R' Assi was there, like Rabbah. Although they did not say where they found that he went, they relied on their aforementioned Eruvin statement drawn from the end of Ketubbot. Yet this needs examination: whence do Tosafot know Rabbah went to the Land of Israel? The aforementioned end of Ketubbot does not explicitly say he went. It says his brothers sent to Rabbah in Babylonia to come to the Land of Israel: ‘Learning on one's own is not like learning from one's teacher. If you say you have no teacher, you do have one: R' Yohanan. If you do not come, take care about three matters,’ etc. Whence this prophetic knowledge that Rabbah went to the Land of Israel? If it is because we find ‘Rabbah said that R' Yohanan said,’ Shabbat 94, end of a; Ta'anit 29a; Sotah 35a—and I have seen some interpreters of the sugya say that speaking in someone's name means he was his teacher—I have already shown in the introductory Rules that this is no proof. Moreover we find ‘Rava said that R' Yohanan said’ (see there), and Tosafot themselves write that Rava did not go to the Land of Israel. I also wrote in Part I (see above) that R' Yohanan and Rav Yehudah died on the same day, and Rava was born on the day Rav Yehudah died; Rava therefore did not see R' Yohanan, yet spoke in his name. Perhaps Tosafot derived it from Rav Hisda telling Rabbah, ‘Who listens to you and to your teacher R' Yohanan?’ Shevuot 10b; Nedarim 59a has Rav Hisda telling Rava, ‘Who listens to you and to your teacher R' Yohanan?’—in my view a scribal error for Rabbah. ‘Your teacher R' Yohanan’ indicates that he went and learned from him. Yet it is difficult: Tosafot should have proved Rabbah's journey from Rav Hisda's ‘your teacher R' Yohanan,’ whereas they wrote ‘as found at the end of Ketubbot.’ Several years after writing this, I saw Maharit, end of Ketubbot: ‘Tosafot in Pasin and He-Arel write that Rabbah went to the Land of Israel, as this passage implies. This passage does not imply that he went. Moreover, the end of Horayot shows he presided twenty-two years and lived only forty, so he was eighteen when he began presiding. Earlier they would not have written, “Although you are a great sage, learning on one's own is not like learning from one's teacher; if you say you have no teacher,” since his teacher Rav Yehudah was alive. If he had died, Rabbah could have learned from many sages in the Land of Israel other than R' Yohanan, since he was young. When the public needed him he began presiding, and presumably did not go. It is more reasonable to say that it was of Abaye that he said, “I saw your head among the rows of pupils”’—see Rav Dimi bar Yosef and understand. ‘But the episode at the beginning of Ellu Megallehin is difficult: Rav Yehudah excommunicated a man with a bad reputation, and Rav Yehudah died. They told him, “There is no great man like Rav Yehudah to release you; go to R' Yehudah Nesia”’ (see Rav Yehudah), ‘and he went. This implies R' Yohanan had already died before Rav Yehudah. How, then, did they send “If you say you have no teacher,” etc.?’ End quotation. That is: since he went to R' Yehudah Nesia to release the excommunication, why did he not go to R' Yohanan, a great man like Rav Yehudah? Necessarily R' Yohanan had already died before Rav Yehudah. When they sent Rabbah word that he had a teacher, R' Yohanan, Rav Yehudah was therefore alive. How could they write, ‘Learning on one's own is not like learning from one's teacher; if you say you are learning on your own because you have no teacher,’ when his teacher Rav Yehudah was alive? One may answer that Rav Yehudah died before R' Yohanan, and therefore his brothers sent him word to come to the Land of Israel to study before R' Yohanan. Why, then, did the man not go to R' Yohanan to release the excommunication? One may answer that Jerusalem Talmud, Ellu Megallehin, says: if the excommunicator dies, they do not release him. This applies where there is no nasi; where there is a nasi, the nasi releases him (see R' Yehudah Nesia, what I wrote there). Thus even if R' Yohanan was alive, he had specifically to go to R' Yehudah Nesia. Understand this. Ra'avad—and Tzeidah La-Derekh in its introduction—writes that Rabbah composed Midrash Rabbah (see R' Hoshaya Rabbah). Rashi, Vayigash, on ‘He took from the end’ (Genesis 47:2) [Heilprin cites Miketz], writes that Bereshit Rabbah is aggadah of the Land of Israel. This needs examination, since it is uncertain whether Rabbah was there. One may answer that although he headed an academy in Pumbedita in Babylonia, he gathered and collected all the aggadot of the Land of Israel (צ״ד [provisionally Tzeidah La-Derekh], 4060).

(2) He was careful about tzitzit: Kol Kitvei, 118, end of b. He erred: this was said of Rava; see Rav Yosef bar Rava. Rabbah is a scribal error. He split wood in honor of Shabbat: there, 119a. There were sixty תיכלי [provisionally “bereavements”] in his house, and he was poor: Mo'ed Katan 28a. Bava Metzia, Ha-Sokher Et Ha-Po'alim, 86a: they told the king that each year he kept thirteen thousand Israelites idle in Adar and Elul [as in Sherira’s Epistle. The checked Bavli reads twelve thousand and specifies that they were unavailable for the royal tax. Rashi names Nisan and Tishrei.]. He fled. A royal official happened to come to Rabbah's lodging. They gave him two cups to drink and removed the table from before him; he was harmed by drinking in pairs, and his face turned backward. The inn's people asked Rabbah, ‘What shall we do? He is the king's man.’ He told them, ‘Bring the table before him and give him one cup.’ They did so, and he recovered. He said, ‘I know the man I seek is here.’ He searched for him and found him. He said, ‘I will leave; even if they kill me, I will not disclose him. But if they flog me, I will disclose him.’ The official put Rabbah in a room and slammed the door before him. Rabbah prayed, broke down the wall, fled to the marsh, and studied. In the heavenly academy they disputed: if the bright spot preceded, etc.; in a doubtful case the Holy One, blessed be He, says ‘pure,’ and the whole academy says ‘impure.’ Who will decide? Rabbah bar Nahmani, unique in Nega'im and Ohalot. They sent a messenger after him, but the Angel of Death could not approach because his mouth never ceased studying. Meanwhile a wind blew and rustled the reeds. He thought it was a troop of cavalry and said, ‘Let that man's soul rest, rather than be handed to the government.’ As his soul departed he said, ‘Pure, pure.’ A heavenly voice issued: ‘Happy are you, whose body is pure and whose soul departed in purity.’ In Pumbedita, a note fell from Heaven [see Rav Sherira Gaon’s Epistle as cited in Yuhasin]: ‘Rabbah bar Nahmani has been summoned to the academy above.’ Abaye and all the rabbis went to attend to him, but did not know his location. They went to the marsh, where birds hovered and stood. They said, ‘Learn from this that he is there.’ They eulogized him three days and three nights. A note fell: ‘Anyone who withdraws shall be excommunicated.’ They eulogized him seven days. A note fell: ‘Go home in peace.’ On the day he died there was a storm wind, which lifted an Arab riding a camel from one bank of the Pappa River and threw him onto the other.

(3) He was an uprooter of mountains: end of Horayot (see Rav Yosef). Rashi, Bava Kamma 33b: Rabbah is an important man; we raise objections from an important man, such as Rav and Rabbah, as if it were written in a Mishnah. The halakhah follows Rabbah against Rav Yosef—Tosafot, Sho'el 148b, see above—except ‘field’ (some read ‘Sodom,’ Bava Batra 12), ‘matter’ (some read ‘acquisition,’ Bava Batra 114), and ‘half’ (Bava Batra 143). See Tosafot, Bava Metzia 29a; Tosafot, Kiddushin 9a, record a view that this applies specifically in Bava Batra. Responsa Havvot Yair writes that this appears so, since we hold ‘Sinai is preferable.’ See Tosafot, Bava Kamma 56b. But Gittin 74b implies this applies everywhere. Rosh, end of Ba-Meh Madlikin, in R' Yonah's name—this is Rabbenu Yonah, since She'erit Yosef, 38b, brings it in his name—says it applies specifically where they disagree on their own authority. Responsa Havvot Yair writes: ‘In my view this is why it was necessary to rule like Rabbah at the end of Berakhot's first chapter: the earlier authorities had already disagreed there [Heilprin has ר״ג and ר״א. The checked Havvot Yair reads Rav and Rav Hisda, while the Rosh there cites Rav and Rabbi Elazar.]; see Asheri.’ He was called King Shapur because the halakhah follows him against Rav Yosef except in three matters: Yesh Nohalin, 115; see Rashbam there. Rif, Bava Metzia's first chapter, concerning witnesses conferring rights through their signatures, writes: Rabbah is Abaye's teacher, and the halakhah does not follow a pupil against his teacher (see above, Rava, halakhic ruling). Hinei and Shilei are near Pumbedita, where Rabbah and Rav Yosef sat (see there). Ivtzan and Avdon ben Hillel the Pirathonite were Rabbah and Rav Hisda (see there) [reported identity interpretation].

(4) Abba bar Marta was in his time. Abaye was his pupil. Shabbat, end of Sho'el: Abaye asked him, ‘Master, whom Pumbedita hates—who will warm your eulogy?’ He answered, ‘You and Rabbah bar Rav Hanan’ (see there). Abaye bar Avin was his pupil. Rav Aha bar Tahlifa in his name. Rav Aha bar Huna. R' Ammi said: Shabbat 125b. Rav Assi called him ‘Rabbi’—needs examination. Rav Ashi said. Rav Ashi told him, ‘But Ulla said.’ Rav Huna was his teacher. Rav Huna bar Sehora. They told him, ‘When you go to Rav Hisda at Kafri, ask him.’ When he came to Sura, Rav Hamnuna spoke to him: Bava Metzia 6b. Rav Zutra bar Shmuel was in his time. He slaughtered R' Zeira at the Purim feast (see there). Ze'iri said. Rav Haviva bar Rav Yosef bar Rava in his name. R' Hiyya said. He went to R' Hiyya bar Huna. R' Hiyya, Rav Yosef's father, was his colleague. R' Hiyya was his son. R' Hiyya bar Ashi in his name. R' Hama bar Buzi before him. Rav Hisda was his teacher or colleague (see above, Rav Hamnuna): Tosafot, Shabbat 123b, beginning ‘A decree.’ R' Hanina bar Avin was his pupil. R' Hanina Hanina'ah spoke to him. Rav Yehudah was his teacher. Rav Yehudah said that Shmuel said: Shabbat 34b, 143b; Pesahim 110, end of b. He asked Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah (see above). R' Yohanan said (see above whether he was his pupil). Rav Yosef was his teacher: Ketubbot 42. In Eruvin 51a he called Rav Yosef ‘master’; there, Eruvin 78a–b, Rav Yosef asked him [Heilprin reports the reverse direction]. When Rabbah died, Rav Yosef sat at the head (see there). Rashi, Bava Metzia 86a, calls Rav Yosef his disputant. Rav Yosef bar Hiyya was his colleague. Rav Yeimar bar Hashu was in his time. R' Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta said. Also Rav Yitzhak bar Rav Yehudah. R' Yitzhak bar Avin was in his time. Rav Kahana said. Rav Kahana the Second was his pupil. Rav Menashya bar Yehudah was in his time. He sent to Mari bar Mar through Abaye. R' Mattana said. R' Nehemya asked him. Rav Nahman bar Hisda sent to him. He challenged Rav Nahman, who called him ‘Abba,’ a title of rabbinic honor: Pesahim 40a. He sat with Rav Yosef at the end of Rav Nahman's lecture: Yevamot 66b. Rav Sehora (see there). Speaking to Abaye, he called Rav Safra ‘our colleague.’ Ukvan bar Nahmani told him in Shmuel's name. Ulla said. Rav said: Gittin 38b. Tosafot, Arakhin 7a: Rabbah lived many years after Rav. Rava was his son. Rava was his pupil. Rava bar Ittai. With Rav bar bar Hana. Rabbah bar Mattana. Rabbah bar R' Hanan (see above). Rami bar Shmuel. He used to challenge Rami bar Hama. Rav Sheizvi asked him. Rav Shmuel bar bar Hana. In Shmuel's name. He was with Rav Yosef at Rav Sheshet's exposition. In R' Shimon's name: the Holy One, blessed be He, prepares a dressing before the wound; Shir Ha-Shirim Rabbah.
